newsitem.title: POLAND: POLISH PREMIER WEIGHS PROTEST TO RUSSIA OVER SHIP.
newsitem.headline: POLISH PREMIER WEIGHS PROTEST TO RUSSIA OVER SHIP.

text.p: Poland may officially protest to Moscow over the detention of a fishing trawler but must not let itself be provoked into harming its NATO entry bid, Prime Minister Wlodzimierz Cimoszewicz said on Tuesday.
Cimoszewicz said the cabinet would have to decide at its meeting during the day whether the time had come for an official protest to the Russian government over the trawler Aquarius.
"I have the feeling this time has arrived," Cimoszewicz told a public radio interviewer.

The ship was arrested on February 26 by Russian fishery protection and border officials on the sea of Okhotsk and forced to sail under armed guard to Pietropavlovsk in Kamchatka, where it continued to be held on Tuesday.
Senior Polish officials said that following their appeals Russian central government leaders, including Prime Minister Viktor Chernomyrdin, agreed to order the ship's release.
But local authorities on the far east Russian peninsula failed to free it, they said.

Although Cimoszewicz said there were arguments for more intensive protests, he warned against falling into a possible trap designed to increase tension just as Poland draws closer to its key goal of joining NATO.

"At the same time we don't want more tension with Russia, because it cannot be ruled out that the whole incident with the Aquarius emerges not from chaos...but because someone in Russia wants a worsening of our relations with Russia," he said.

"We would not want to contribute to such an eventual scenario, as we want good relations with Russia...remember that in several months decisions will fall in the most important matters for Poland, including our NATO membership," he said.
Poland expects to be invited at NATO's Madrid summit in July to start talks on joining the pact, even though Russia opposes the move as a threat to its security.

Warsaw is conscious that Western critics of NATO enlargement argue the move will unnecessarily increase tension with Russia and it is keen to cultivate good ties with Moscow, partly to undermine such arguments.

Cimoszewicz, who called the whole Aquarius episode astonishing, said he wanted to believe that it stemmed from the current chaos in Russia's administration and that authorities on Kamchatka were acting against central government orders.

Russian officials, who say the ship began fishing a day earlier than its permits allowed and allege other irregularities in its documentation, want to fine the vessel and confiscate its catch, according to Polish reports.
The ship's owners deny any wrongdoing, argue that the arrest infringed a fishery agreeement between the two countries and want compensation from Russia for losses. -- Anthony Barker +48 22 653 9700
